title: The Print Two Dealers Can't Agree Is a Landscape
standfirst: This 1967 etching is catalogued by Tate as a landscape and, by a London print dealer selling an impression from the same edition, as Two Goblets and a Beaker. Ben Nicholson spent decades engineering exactly that confusion — and denied, on the record, that any of it came from Cubism, the label still attached to his name.

sections.heading: Two Names for the Same Plate
sections.body: Tate holds this print as *3 forms in a landscape*, dated 1967 and [catalogued as an etching on paper](https://www.tate.org.uk/art/artworks/nicholson-3-forms-in-a-landscape-p02016) — not a painting, whatever else gets filed alongside it. A London dealer selling an impression from the identical run gives the date as 1968 and [notes in passing](https://www.modernprints.co.uk/products/ben-nicholson-three-forms-in-a-landscape-1) that the same image is also known as Two Goblets and a Beaker. Both are describing one fifty-copy edition, printed in Locarno and published in London by Ganymed Original Editions and Marlborough Fine Art. Nobody involved seems troubled that a single plate can be a hillside to one cataloguer and a shelf of glassware to another.

sections.heading: A Habit Twenty Years Old Already
sections.body: By 1947 Nicholson had a name for what he was doing: pictures where a tabletop of bottles and goblets dissolves into a distant hillside, a device he called his still life-landscapes, [documented in one gallery's own account](https://pallant-assets.s3.amazonaws.com/uploads/2021/07/Ben-Nicholson-Wall-Text-and-Labels_Handout_SJ-edits.pdf) of his career. It was already two decades old by the time he turned it into an etching. A closely related plate from the same year, two goblets and a mug in a landscape, [now held by a Scottish national collection](https://pallant-assets.s3.amazonaws.com/uploads/2021/07/Ben-Nicholson-Wall-Text-and-Labels_Handout_SJ-edits.pdf), plays the identical trick with vessels that could just as easily be forms standing in open country. He had used a version of the same title once before, [on a smaller plate made a year earlier](https://www.redfern-gallery.com/artists/235-ben-nicholson/works/11781/).

sections.heading: Not Cubism, He Said — My Father's Jugs
sections.body: The corpus files this etching under Cubism, the label it gives most of Nicholson's mature work. Nicholson [pushed back on exactly that lineage](https://pallant-assets.s3.amazonaws.com/uploads/2021/07/Ben-Nicholson-Wall-Text-and-Labels_Handout_SJ-edits.pdf), on the record: "In my work, this theme did not originally come from cubism, as some people think, but from my father — not only from what he made as a painter, but from the very beautiful striped and spotted jugs and mugs and goblets, and octagonal and hexagonal glass objects he collected. Having those things in the house was an unforgettable early experience for me." His father was an established Edwardian portrait and still-life painter; Nicholson's own first attempts at painting, done in that same representational manner, he later dismissed as "slick" and "Vermeer." It was the objects his father kept in the house, not the movement his son is filed under, that Nicholson credited with the etching now in front of you.

sections.heading: The Cubism He Did Keep
sections.body: He wasn't wrong to admire Cubism — he was correcting which debt it created. In the 1930s Nicholson made a point of visiting Paris, meeting Picasso and Braque directly and touring the studios of Arp, Brâncuși and Mondrian. He kept a guitar in his own studio for the same reason Braque kept instruments in his: it was, [in the words of one gallery's wall text](https://pallant-assets.s3.amazonaws.com/uploads/2021/07/Ben-Nicholson-Wall-Text-and-Labels_Handout_SJ-edits.pdf), a central theme worth drawing over and over. Between 1945 and 1958 Nicholson was still producing what [one specialist dealer's account of his career calls](https://www.piano-nobile.com/artists/70-ben-nicholson/biography/) "sophisticated cubistic still-life paintings," large-scale work that won him the first Guggenheim International Award in 1956. The label isn't baseless. It just belongs to an earlier decade and a different material — by 1967 the canvas had become a copper plate, the brush a steel point, and the studio a house above a Swiss lake.

sections.heading: Prepared in Locarno, Engraved Above the Lake
sections.body: What the print itself can't show is the traffic behind it. Between 1965 and 1969 — [his most sustained stretch as a printmaker](https://pallant-assets.s3.amazonaws.com/uploads/2021/07/Ben-Nicholson-Wall-Text-and-Labels_Handout_SJ-edits.pdf) — Nicholson worked with the Swiss printer François Lafranca, who cut and prepared blank copper plates in Ticino and sent them up to the house Nicholson had built above Lake Maggiore [after leaving Cornwall in 1958](https://www.piano-nobile.com/artists/70-ben-nicholson/biography/). Nicholson engraved the plates there and shipped them back down for printing; he thought of the results as "drawings on copper" rather than etchings proper. Of the medium itself he wrote: "Etchings … are irresistible to do because of the bite of the hard point & the golden glitter that happens on the dark-as-night plate. It is like cutting, which a pen or pencil is not." He described the move to Switzerland in the same register, writing to his first wife that the new house was "so beautiful that one can hardly believe it — & the landscape contains lots of work in it for me."

sections.heading: Fifty Copies, Loosely Dated
sections.body: The edition ran to fifty, published in London — a number that put a late Nicholson image into far more houses than any single one of his unique paintings could. It also explains why the record is untidy. Tate's own impression is dated 1967; [a dealer's impression from the identical plate](https://www.modernprints.co.uk/products/ben-nicholson-three-forms-in-a-landscape-1) carries a pencil date of 1968, the year Nicholson was appointed to the Order of Merit and became, [by one account](https://www.piano-nobile.com/artists/70-ben-nicholson/biography/), one of the few British modernists to win international recognition in his own lifetime. Nobody involved seems to have thought the discrepancy worth resolving. For a printmaker who signed sheets as they were pulled, sometimes a year or more after engraving the plate, a one-year gap between two catalogue entries barely counts as a disagreement at all.
